tagline: A shore loop crosses South Cove and passes Fenwick’s golf course.
intro: The southern loop of Route 154 follows Long Island Sound and crosses South Cove, linking Saybrook Manor, Fenwick and Old Saybrook Center. The 6.10 miles from Saybrook Manor to the east junction with Old Boston Post Road form a state scenic road. Fenwick sits where the Connecticut River enters the Sound, separated from the town center by a cove and causeway.

This loop began its numbered life as State Highway 338 in 1922 and became Route 154 in 1932. The original route returned from Fenwick along Maple Avenue. In 1935, the western side moved onto Plum Bank Road and Great Hammock Road, establishing the present alignment. The highway’s role expanded in 1967, when the opening of the Route 9 freeway transferred an old surface-road section to Route 154. That extension ran from US 1 to Essex Road in Old Saybrook, beyond the original shore loop.

From US 1, drive south along Great Hammock Road and Plum Bank Road, then east through Knollwood to Fenwick. The road passes the golf course and crosses South Cove before turning sharply west onto College Street. Main Street then turns north beside North Cove toward the loop’s end at Old Boston Post Road.

moments.title: Fenwick
moments.text: Shingle-style houses give Fenwick’s historic district much of its architectural character. Seventeen of its 60 main buildings represent that style, with others in Queen Anne and Victorian styles. Look for flared eaves, upper floors extending beyond the walls below, and small roofs over doors and windows. The golf course took shape from empty lots in the late 1800s. Its nine holes have been rearranged several times, most recently in the 1930s. St. Mary’s-By-the-Sea, built in 1883, shares the district’s flared eaves and overhanging forms. Most of Fenwick falls within the historic district, which entered the National Register in 1995.

moments.title: Lynde Point lighthouses
moments.text: Two lights mark the harbor channel at the Connecticut River’s mouth: Lynde Point’s Inner Light and the Saybrook Breakwater Outer Light. The Inner Light began as a 35-foot wooden tower completed in 1803. Sailors found the original tower too short to see effectively, a problem worsened by fog from the marshland. It was replaced by a 65-foot octagonal brownstone tower, built in 1838 and first lit in 1839. Painted white, the replacement has six windows, all facing the water. The sparkplug-shaped Outer Light appears on Connecticut’s Preserve the Sound license plates.
moments.notice: The Inner Light’s six windows all face the water.

moments.title: Old Saybrook
moments.text: At Saybrook Point, railroad remains occupy part of the site of Fort Saybrook. The Connecticut Valley Railroad began service between the point and Hartford in 1871, the year it built its roundhouse and turntable here. The extension to the point closed in 1922, and the facilities were abandoned. Excavations in 1981–82 exposed the surviving remains. In Fort Saybrook Monument Park, portions of the roundhouse’s brick-and-stone foundations and the turntable’s concrete base are exposed, with signs explaining their use. The wider railroad complex once included an icehouse, coal bin, steamboat dock, depot and signal tower; the roundhouse and turntable are its only surviving remnant.
